33713719.reason: A pooled average ignores the no-mixed-cake condition: the first and second cake each need a positive separate plate count. Pooling makes it impossible to enforce the lower bound on every plate.

counterexample.derivation: For n=4, a=7, b=10, a minimum of 4 would allow at most floor(7/4)=1 first-cake plate and floor(10/4)=2 second-cake plates, fewer than four. Minimum 3 is attained by first-cake plates of 3,4 and second-cake plates of 5,5. Hence the optimum is 3, not pooled floor(17/4)=4.
counterexample.normalization: Only CRLF to LF in an audit copy; original package preserved.

semanticReview.faultyLogic: A pooled average ignores the no-mixed-cake condition: the first and second cake each need a positive separate plate count. Pooling makes it impossible to enforce the lower bound on every plate.
semanticReview.implementedAlgorithm: Reads plate and cake quantities, pools both cakes, and prints floor((a+b)/n).

33713862.reason: Each cake should be divided among its own subset of plates rather than both cakes divided by n. Also at total pieces exactly n its zero-sum correction fails, despite every plate being able to get one piece.

counterexample.derivation: For n=5, a=2, b=3 the total number of pieces equals five plates, so all five plates must have exactly one piece. Assign two plates to the first cake and three to the second: optimum 1. The source computes floor(2/5)+floor(3/5)=0 and its strict total>n correction is false, printing 0.
counterexample.normalization: Only CRLF to LF in an audit copy; original package preserved.

33713938.reason: It checks only total capacity, allowing one cake to supply zero plates and disappear. A valid allocation needs at least one plate for each positive cake; the candidate minimum must not exceed min(a,b).

counterexample.derivation: For n=10, a=100, b=3 the three-piece cake needs at least one nonempty plate, bounding the minimum by 3. Give its sole plate 3 and split the other cake among nine plates (eight 11-piece plates and one 12-piece plate), attaining 3. The capacity scan permits zero second-cake plates for k>3, keeps k=10 because 100/10+3/10=10, and exits at 11 with answer 10.
counterexample.normalization: Only CRLF to LF in an audit copy; original package preserved.

33713943.reason: The endpoint allocations i=0 and i=n illegally discard all pieces of one positive cake. Optimizing over those illegal endpoints can greatly exceed the best legal minimum.

counterexample.derivation: For n=10, a=100, b=3 at least one plate must hold second-cake pieces, so the minimum is at most 3. One such plate with 3 and nine first-cake plates of 11 or 12 attain 3. The illegal i=n endpoint uses only a and reports 100/10=10, discarding all three b pieces.
